Baby & Child

Newborn cone-shaped head: normal moulding and when to seek care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Meeting your newborn can bring delight and worry at the same time, especially when their head looks longer or more pointed than expected. Temporary moulding after birth is common, but a photograph cannot establish that every unusual shape or lump is harmless. This guide explains birth-related changes, safe ways to vary awake activity, and when to ask your baby’s care team for help.

Why a newborn’s head can look cone-shaped

A newborn’s skull consists of separate bones with flexible seams called sutures and soft areas called fontanelles. During passage through the birth canal, the bones can shift and overlap temporarily. This moulding can produce a long or pointed head and small overlapping ridges. Normal moulding by itself does not mean brain damage.

The effect may be more noticeable after a long labour or when the baby has been low in the pelvis before birth. Babies born by caesarean often have less moulding, particularly without labour, but birth position and labour still matter. Neither the delivery method nor a prenatal three- or four-dimensional scan guarantees a particular head shape; a fixed comparison between head and cervical diameter is not useful for judging an individual baby.

How long moulding lasts and what soft spots mean

Birth moulding often starts improving over the first days, with further rounding over the following weeks. There is no exact 48-hour deadline or promise that every shape will correct itself. Ask the midwife or clinician to examine a shape that concerns you, is worsening, or is not improving as expected; do not wait months solely because someone called it normal.

Fontanelles and sutures allow the skull to grow with the brain. Different spaces close at different ages, and a soft spot can normally pulse with the heartbeat. Gentle everyday washing and handling are safe; support the head and neck, and do not press or massage the skull into shape. The claim that all skull growth spaces remain open until adolescence is not a reason to dismiss a persistent abnormal shape.

Birth moulding, positional flattening and early suture closure differ

A cone-shaped head immediately after birth differs from flattening that develops when a young baby repeatedly rests on the same part of the head. Positional plagiocephaly may flatten one side; brachycephaly may flatten the back. A preferred head direction, limited neck movement or prematurity can contribute. Confirmed positional flattening does not itself damage the brain, but a clinician should establish the cause.

Less commonly, an unusual shape reflects a suture that has fused too early, called craniosynostosis; some forms occur with a genetic condition. Persistent or progressive asymmetry, an unusual ridge or concerns about head growth need assessment. A photo, an open soft spot or a parent’s touch cannot reliably rule this out. Injury is another reason for a new change to be checked, rather than assumed to be birth moulding.

Keep back sleeping for every nap and night

Place your newborn on their back for every sleep, on a firm, flat, level mattress in an approved cot or bassinet with a fitted sheet. Keep the sleep space clear of pillows, head-shaping cushions, positioners, loose bedding and toys. Room-share with a separate baby sleep space. Head shape is not a reason to use side or tummy sleeping or an inclined surface.

Swings, bouncers, car seats, slings and carriers are not substitutes for a safe sleep surface. If your baby falls asleep in one, move them onto their back on an appropriate firm, flat surface as soon as possible. Use a car seat correctly for travel, not as routine head-shaping treatment. Do not fall asleep holding the baby on a sofa or armchair.

Vary awake activity without forcing the head

Offer short, frequent periods of tummy time while your baby is awake and an awake adult watches closely. Start gently and build up according to tolerance; early sessions can be on your chest only when you are fully awake and unlikely to fall asleep. Tummy time supports neck and upper-body development and relieves pressure on the back of the head. If the baby becomes sleepy, return them to their safe back-sleeping space.

Vary the arm or side used for feeding and carrying, support the head, and offer faces or age-appropriate toys from different directions during supervised awake play. Keep toys and mobiles out of reach and out of the sleep space. Limit unnecessary time in reclining seats and carriers; holding and safe floor play provide variety. Do not force a neck turn, repeatedly press a flat area or use a swing to reshape the skull.

A head tilt or one-sided feeding preference needs review

Torticollis means a tilted or preferential neck posture. Congenital muscular torticollis involves tightness of the sternocleidomastoid muscle: the head may tilt towards one side while the chin turns away. A baby may prefer feeding on one side, avoid turning towards you or turn their whole body instead. Position in the womb can be relevant, but the cause cannot be established from that history alone.

It can be noticed in the first month; there is no need to wait until head control develops at six to eight weeks. Ask for an examination if the head is persistently tilted or movement is limited. Early clinician-directed positioning and, when needed, physiotherapy can help. Learn any stretches from the treating professional instead of forcing the neck; a new painful tilt, illness or neurological change needs prompt assessment for other causes.

A scalp lump is different from a pointed skull

Caput is fluid-related scalp swelling around delivery that usually settles over the first days. A cephalohaematoma is blood collected beneath the membrane covering a skull bone, outside the brain; it may become apparent after birth and take weeks or months to resolve. These changes can coexist with moulding, but a clinician needs to identify a new lump. Do not diagnose it by pressing, comparing pictures or assuming every post-birth swelling is harmless.

A confirmed cephalohaematoma often needs observation rather than a procedure, but can contribute to jaundice or anaemia and occasionally other complications. Follow the team’s checks for the lump, feeding and jaundice. Do not puncture, drain or massage it at home. Rapidly enlarging or spreading soft swelling can represent a different, serious bleed called subgaleal haemorrhage and needs immediate emergency assessment, particularly if the baby looks pale or unwell.

When to get urgent help

Seek emergency care now for rapidly increasing or spreading scalp swelling, trouble breathing, blue or markedly pale colour, difficulty waking, a seizure, unusual floppiness or serious deterioration. A newborn with a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower needs immediate medical assessment. Do not wait for a routine head-shape appointment, a photograph review or every warning sign to appear.

Contact the maternity or paediatric team urgently for a new unexplained lump, poor feeding, fewer wet nappies, increasing jaundice or a persistently bulging soft spot, especially when the baby is calm. Jaundice in the first 24 hours, or jaundice with poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, abnormal movements or breathing problems, needs emergency assessment. A soft spot that looks sunken with poor feeding or reduced wet nappies may indicate dehydration and also needs medical advice.

Examination, treatment and reassurance

Your care team can review birth history, examine the skull and neck, measure head growth and arrange follow-up. Imaging or specialist referral is chosen when the examination suggests another condition; it is not automatic for ordinary improving moulding. Physiotherapy addresses an identified neck problem. A helmet is not a routine treatment for normal newborn moulding, and head-shaping pillows are unsafe for sleep.

For selected persistent moderate or severe positional deformity, specialist advice about helmet therapy varies: the AAP describes selected use, while the NHS notes insufficient evidence for routine provision. It does not correct fused sutures by itself; suspected craniosynostosis needs a specialist pathway, sometimes including surgery. Enjoy your baby and record questions or gradual changes if helpful, while keeping follow-up and seeking care sooner for new concerns. No parent is expected to diagnose skull conditions at home.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish ordinary birth moulding from positional flattening, neck restriction, scalp bleeding and early suture closure.

Current AAP, CDC and NHS guidance keeps back sleeping and a firm, flat, clear sleep surface; supervised awake tummy time is a separate activity.

Care follows the baby’s examination, growth and symptoms; persistent shape changes or new lumps cannot be cleared by an image alone.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record questions, feeding concerns and the timing of visible changes for your care team. It cannot diagnose skull fusion, distinguish scalp bleeds or declare a newborn safe from a photograph. Do not delay urgent care to measure, track or upload an image.

When to seek help

Use safe back sleeping for every sleep. Get emergency help for spreading scalp swelling, breathing difficulty, marked pallor or blue colour, difficulty waking, seizures or a severely unwell newborn. Temperature abnormalities or jaundice with illness need immediate assessment. New lumps, poor feeding or persistent head-shape concerns need professional review. This information does not replace individual newborn care.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Temporary birth moulding is common, but persistent, worsening or unexplained changes need an examination.
  • Use back sleeping on a firm, flat, clear surface for every nap and night; tummy time is awake and supervised only.
  • Vary safe awake play, feeding and carrying; do not force the neck or reshape the skull by pressure.
  • New scalp lumps need identification; spreading swelling or an unwell newborn needs immediate care.

Frequently asked questions

Is a cone-shaped head normal after birth?

Temporary moulding is common, especially after vaginal birth. The skull bones can overlap during delivery. A clinician should confirm the explanation when the shape is unusual, worsening or accompanied by swelling or illness.

How long should the cone shape last?

Improvement often begins in the first days and continues over weeks, but there is no exact deadline or guarantee. Ask for assessment if it is not improving as expected, rather than relying on claims about skull closure in adolescence.

What else can change a baby’s head shape?

Repeated pressure, a preferred head direction, tight neck muscles and prematurity can contribute to positional flattening. Less common causes include early suture fusion, genetic conditions or injury. An examination distinguishes these from birth moulding.

What can I safely do to help the shape?

Keep back sleeping. During awake supervised time, vary feeding and carrying sides and offer short tummy-time sessions. Do not use pillows, positioners, tummy sleeping or prolonged time in swings and seats as head-shaping treatments.

Is a new lump definitely a harmless cephalohaematoma?

No. A clinician must identify the swelling. Confirmed cephalohaematomas often resolve with observation but need follow-up for complications such as jaundice. Rapidly spreading swelling or a pale, unwell baby needs emergency care.

Should I wait until my baby can control their head before checking a tilt?

No. Persistent tilt, difficulty turning or one-sided feeding preference can be assessed early. Follow professional advice about positioning and any exercises; do not force stretches yourself.

Does normal newborn moulding need a helmet?

Usually no. Ordinary improving moulding needs observation and routine care. Selected persistent positional flattening may need specialist discussion; early fused sutures need a different pathway. Do not buy a helmet or shaping pillow without appropriate advice.

Which signs mean I should not wait?

Emergency signs include spreading scalp swelling, breathing difficulty, marked pallor or blue colour, difficulty waking, seizures or major deterioration. A newborn’s fever or low temperature, early jaundice or jaundice with illness also needs immediate assessment. Seek urgent advice for poor feeding, reduced wet nappies or a new lump.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
